somalia.content: Famine Risk in Baidoa Averted, but 5.3 Million Somalis Still Face Acute Food Insecurity - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Environment & Climate South West State Famine Risk in Baidoa Averted, but 5.3 Million Somalis Still Face Acute Food Insecurity November 26, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , The risk of famine among internally displaced people in Baidoa has been averted, according to an updated IPC projection published on November 25, but 5.3 million people across Somalia are still projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity between October and December 2026, including nearly 1.5 million in Emergency conditions. The update, which revises the August 2026 projection, confirms that Baidoa’s displaced population remains in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) for food insecurity and Phase 4 (Critical) for acute malnutrition through December. However, the plausible worst-case scenario of extreme El Niño-induced flooding and mass displacement that could have pushed the population into famine has not materialized and is unlikely to occur before the end of the year, according to the report. What Changed Since August The revised projection for Baidoa IDPs shows modest improvements. In August, 80 percent of Baidoa’s displaced population was projected to face Crisis or worse conditions, with 5 percent in Catastrophe. The November analysis estimates that 65 percent now face Crisis or worse, and no population is projected to face Catastrophe. Three factors drove the improvement. Flood displacement remained far below projections, with approximately 42,000 people displaced compared with the 89,000 anticipated in August. Improved access to agricultural labor and income strengthened purchasing power for some households. And food prices, while still above average, declined enough to ease pressure on the poorest families. New displacements into Baidoa were also substantially lower than anticipated. Insecurity in the city generated an estimated 5,600 new displacements following September clashes, but that increase was more than offset by the absence of major flood displacement, a threat FTL Somalia tracked as the Deyr season approached. As a result of the revised Baidoa figures, the national estimate has been slightly revised downward to 5.3 million people facing IPC Phase 3 or above, from 5.4 million projected in August. Of those, 3.88 million are in Crisis and 1.46 million are in Emergency. Malnutrition Burden Grows Despite the improved food security outlook, acute malnutrition remains a major concern. The updated analysis estimates that 1.92 million children aged 6 to 59 months will require treatment for acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027, including 437,000 cases of severe acute malnutrition. An additional 155,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women are also acutely malnourished and in need of treatment. The malnutrition figures were revised upward slightly, by 7,000 cases for Baidoa IDPs, following a new SMART nutrition survey conducted in late October. Nearly 62 percent of all acute malnutrition cases are concentrated in southern Somalia, driven by limited access to health and nutrition services, disease outbreaks, food insecurity, and poor water and sanitation. The report notes that child feeding practices remain a critical risk factor. Only 3.8 percent of children have minimum dietary diversity, and only 2.3 percent consume a minimum acceptable diet. Exclusive breastfeeding stands at 33 percent, well below the recommended level. Disease burden is also high, with measles reporting at 259 percent of the long-term average and diarrhea at 142 percent. Aid Reaches a Fraction of Those in Need The most troubling figure in the report is not the number of people facing hunger. It is the number receiving help. Humanitarian food security assistance from October to December 2026 will reach only 70,000 people per month, or 0.4 percent of the total population, despite 5.3 million people requiring assistance. Funding constraints have also forced the closure of 233 nutrition sites and 380 health facilities across the country, reducing the capacity to prevent and treat malnutrition. In Baidoa, the scale-up of health and nutrition services since October, including two additional health facilities and four outreach sites, has helped prevent a further deterioration. But that scale-up is a local exception in a national context of retrenchment. Compounding the problem, the Deyr season is expected to bring average to above-average rainfall across most of Somalia due to El Niño, with a 90 percent chance of above-normal rainfall in central and southern regions. While this may improve pasture and agricultural conditions in some areas, it also raises the risk of flooding in riverine livelihoods and low-lying settlements, which could displace populations and disrupt markets. FTL Critical Note The IPC update is, on its face, good news. Famine has been averted in Baidoa. The worst-case scenario did not materialize. The national hunger estimate fell slightly. These are real improvements, and they reflect the resilience of Somali communities and the efforts of humanitarian workers who have operated under severe constraints. But the report also documents a crisis that is deepening in ways that the headline numbers obscure. The number of acutely malnourished children has increased, not decreased. The closure of 233 nutrition sites and 380 health facilities means that fewer children will receive the treatment they need. And the humanitarian food security assistance reaching 0.4 percent of the population is not a response to a food crisis. It is a gesture. The famine was averted because the rains did not fail and the floods did not come. That is not a policy achievement. It is luck. The underlying drivers of hunger, including conflict, displacement, high food prices, and the lingering effects of drought, remain unaddressed. The government’s own grain production report found that 85 percent of the country’s harvest is concentrated in three southern regions. The El Niño forecast remains active. And the funding for the humanitarian response is shrinking, not growing. The IPC report’s most important conclusion is not that famine was averted. It is that 5.3 million people are still in crisis, 1.46 million of them in emergency, and the international community is reaching almost none of them. A crisis that is not a famine is still a crisis. The absence of the worst outcome does not mean the presence of an adequate response. The three ministers met Saturday, Nov. 21, on the sidelines of the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development in Egypt, where they discussed regional security challenges, maritime navigation and political cooperation among countries in the Horn of Africa. advertisements According to a statement from Egypt's Foreign Ministry, the meeting brought together Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem and Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh. The ministers emphasized the importance of respecting Somalia's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity and expressed opposition to the establishment of parallel entities that could undermine the country's state institutions. The statement did not identify any specific administration or political group in connection with its rejection of parallel entities. The ministers also agreed to strengthen consultation and coordination on issues of mutual concern, building on agreements reached during a four-country summit held in Egypt last month. The October summit in New Alamein brought together the leaders of Egypt, Somalia and Eritrea, along with Sudan's military leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, to discuss security, regional cooperation and political developments in the Horn of Africa. During Saturday's meeting, Abdelatty said Egypt would brief Somalia on the discussions as part of efforts to maintain coordination among the four countries. The ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the outcomes of the Alamein summit, emphasizing the importance of closer cooperation to address regional security threats and protect national sovereignty. They also discussed developments in the Red Sea, calling for stronger cooperation to maintain maritime security, protect international shipping routes and ensure freedom of navigation. The ministers stressed that responsibility for governing the Red Sea and safeguarding its security should rest with countries bordering the waterway. Their position reflects growing regional discussions over the security of the Red Sea, a strategically important shipping corridor connecting international trade routes through the Suez Canal and the Gulf of Aden. The three ministers also reaffirmed their support for Sudan's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity amid the country's continuing conflict. They emphasized the importance of preserving Sudan's national institutions and rejected the involvement of armed militias and the provision of weapons to such groups from foreign sources. The ministers similarly expressed support for Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity. They opposed unilateral measures affecting regional security and water resources, stressing that disputes should be addressed through consultation and respect for international law. The discussions also emphasized the principle of noninterference in the internal affairs of states, with the three countries agreeing to maintain coordination aimed at strengthening regional stability and development. Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea have increased diplomatic consultations in recent months amid security and political challenges affecting the Horn of Africa and Red Sea region. somalia.content: Somalia Says Beledweyne Airport Not Permanently Closed, Demands Troop Withdrawal - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Hirshabelle Somalia Says Beledweyne Airport Not Permanently Closed, Demands Troop Withdrawal November 26, 2026 5 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation, Mohamed Farah Nuux, said on Thursday that the government has not permanently closed Beledweyne’s Ugaas Khaliif Airport and will review the security situation before restoring flights, calling for troops to be withdrawn from the facility to create a stable environment for airlines and passengers. “The government has not closed Beledweyne airport, but we will look into the security of that specific area before it is restored,” Nuux said, according to a statement carried by the Somali National News Agency. The minister’s remarks clarify the government’s position after the Somali Civil Aviation Authority issued a Notice to Airmen on November 24 closing the airport to all Instrument Flight Rules and Visual Flight Rules traffic until December 1. The NOTAM did not specify a reason, and the government has now indicated that the closure is temporary and contingent on security conditions rather than a permanent decision, a closure FTL Somalia documented . The Troop Withdrawal Demand Nuux called for security forces to leave the airport premises and for a peaceful environment to be established so that airlines and travelers can operate with confidence. His statement did not specify which forces should withdraw, but the context makes the reference clear. Djiboutian troops serving under AUSSOM have guarded the airport perimeter for years, and the November 19 clash between those troops and local militia fighters erupted when the militia moved toward the airport to prevent an aircraft carrying additional federal troops from landing. The November 23 agreement between federal lawmakers and AUSSOM Sector Four commanders had already stipulated that troops stationed outside the airport premises would be withdrawn and that aircraft carrying additional military personnel would be prohibited from landing. That agreement was intended to allow the airport to reopen. It lasted less than a day before Hirshabelle’s Ministry of Transport and Aviation said security could not be guaranteed because armed groups remained around the facility, prompting the federal NOTAM. The minister’s latest statement appears to reaffirm the terms of that agreement while acknowledging that they have not been implemented. The forces are still there. The armed groups are still there. The airport remains closed. A Reversal of Framing The minister’s remarks represent a shift in how the government is framing the closure. The NOTAM was a technical document that grounded all flights without explanation. The Hirshabelle ministry’s statement blamed armed groups around the facility. Nuux’s statement reframes the closure as a temporary security measure and emphasizes the government’s willingness to facilitate flights for the people of Hiiraan. That reframing may reflect a recognition that a prolonged closure of the airport would carry political and humanitarian costs. Ugaas Khaliif Airport is the primary air link between Beledweyne and Mogadishu. Passengers traveling for medical treatment, business, or family reasons have been forced onto roads where security risks are higher, and humanitarian agencies that rely on air transport face delays. The statement also comes as the December 1 expiration of the NOTAM approaches. The government needed to clarify whether the closure would be extended indefinitely or whether flights would resume. Nuux’s remarks suggest the latter, conditional on security improvements that have not yet materialized. FTL Critical Note The transport minister’s statement is a clarification, not a resolution. It confirms that the airport closure is temporary and that the government intends to reopen it when conditions allow. But it does not explain how those conditions will be met, who is responsible for meeting them, or what timeline the government has in mind. The core problem remains unchanged. The airport is contested because Beledweyne is contested. The local militia and the Hawadle actors aligned with it oppose the Hirshabelle administration and the arrival of additional federal troops, a mobilization FTL Somalia covered as it began. The Djiboutian peacekeepers are caught between those forces, tasked with guarding a facility that has become a symbol of political authority. The November 23 agreement tried to square this circle by withdrawing troops from the perimeter and banning military flights. It failed because the underlying dispute was not addressed, a crisis rooted in Hirshabelle’s unresolved power-sharing arrangements . Nuux’s call for troops to withdraw is a restatement of that agreement, not a new initiative. If the forces do not withdraw, or if the armed groups remain, the airport will stay closed, and the NOTAM will be extended. The government can issue statements about its willingness to facilitate flights. It cannot issue a statement that makes the airport safe. That requires a political settlement in Hiiraan that neither Mogadishu nor Hiiraan’s feuding factions have been able to reach. Until they do, the airport will remain what it has been for the past week: a facility that exists on paper but not in service. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Puntland’s Deni calls Somalia president’s UAE interference claim ‘unfortunate’ Puntland’s Deni calls Somalia president’s UAE interference claim ‘unfortunate’ November 26, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni on Wednesday dismissed Somalia President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s charge of United Arab Emirates interference—framed by some federal officials as an “open invasion”—as an outdated political habit and a source of national embarrassment. The rebuke landed one day after a cabinet the Supreme Court has already confined to caretaker status approved election-law amendments that tilt the field toward the ruling party. Deni cast the accusation as a familiar diversion. When domestic plans reach a dead end, leaders redirect public anger toward outsiders who hold no organic stake in Somali disputes, he said. The country’s fractures—killing and displacement—were made by Somalis and can be closed only by Somalis, he added, stressing that external actors, including the UAE, arrived after those fractures already existed. To ask foreigners to impose agreement, he said, is itself a shame. He reserved sharper language for what he called term-expired officials in Mogadishu. An unagreed constitution, refusal to accept the Supreme Court’s ruling, and the sudden rewriting of election laws form, in his view, a smokescreen. On 5 November the Court held that parliamentary mandate ended on 14 April 2026 and the presidential term on 15 May 2026; the five-year extensions passed earlier this year could not apply retrospectively. Both branches, and the cabinet that derives its authority from parliament, were limited to routine caretaker duties. On Wednesday—hours after the cabinet session—ousted Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed wrote to the prime minister urging strict adherence to that judgment and to constitutional limits. The government has rejected the ruling, removed the chief justice the night before it was delivered, and continued to act as if the extension remained valid. Against this backdrop the cabinet, in an extraordinary session on 24 November, amended 23 articles of the National Elections Law and eight of the parties law. The changes introduce closed party lists: voters select a party rather than individual candidates, and seats go to candidates pre-ranked by the party. A 10 percent national-vote threshold confers national-party status. Citizens would directly elect local councils, federal-member-state assemblies and both houses of parliament; those bodies would then choose higher officials, including the president. A well-resourced ruling party—the Justice and Solidarity Party—can more readily secure a parliamentary majority under closed lists, after which lawmakers select the president. Critics see the design as engineered to clear a lightly contested path for the incumbent. Deni’s most consequential signal was institutional. He stated that Puntland will protect Somali governance and rally the public behind it, and that the legitimate government seated in Puntland is capable of representing all Somalis. The language was widely read as preparation for a parallel national authority—the contingency opposition figures have repeatedly threatened—if Mohamud continues to reject a negotiated exit and insists on a process he alone controls. The exchange crystallises interlocking crises. Domestically, the 2012 federal bargain is under open strain: Puntland and Jubaland have long rejected unilateral constitutional and electoral changes as violations of the compact that ended centralised rule. Regionally, the UAE dispute is not peripheral. Abu Dhabi maintains deep commercial and security ties with Puntland (Bosaso port and maritime forces), Jubaland, and Somaliland (Berbera). Mogadishu’s January annulment of those agreements, followed by the November expulsion of the Emirati ambassador, has been rejected by the regional administrations as beyond federal competence. For international observers the stakes are clear: a prolonged contest over legitimacy between a centre asserting post-term authority and autonomous member states aligned with Gulf partners risks further fragmentation, weaker coordination against Al-Shabaab, and the militarisation of what remains a political dispute. Whether Deni’s signal remains rhetorical or becomes operational now turns on a single question: whether Mogadishu treats the Court’s caretaker limits as binding or continues to legislate its own electoral path. The answer will shape not only the next Somali presidency but the viability of the federal order itself. جماهيره من صعوبة البدايات، ليؤكد عزمه على الاحتفاظ باللقب. النيجيري تايو يفتتح أهداف الهلال في الدوري يدين الهلال بالفضل في هذا الفوز لمحترفه النيجيري أكيري تايو، الذي سجل هدف المباراة الوحيد في الشوط الأول، ليفتتح رصيد فريقه في النسخة الـ31 من الدوري السوداني الممتاز ، متوجًا أفضلية الهلال وتفوقه الميداني الذي عكس جاهزيته البدنية والفنية بعد معسكره التحضيري في العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، في حين اكتفى منافسه بفترة إعداد قصيرة. واستهل المدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت مسيرته بفوز مهم، وذلك بعد توليه قيادة الفريق قبل ساعات فقط من وصوله إلى البلاد. واعتمد المدرب الشاب، البالغ من العمر 29 عامًا فقط، football.summary: استهل فريق الهلال السوداني حملة الدفاع عن لقبه بفوز ثمين على الأهلي مروي بنتيجة 1-0 في الجولة الأولى من الدوري السوداني الممتاز، التي أقيمت على ملعب مدينة كريمة. سجل الهدف الوحيد للمباراة المحترف النيجيري أكيري تايو في الشوط الأول، مما يعكس جاهزية الهلال البدنية والفنية بعد معسكره التحضيري في كيغالي. المدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت، الذي تولى قيادة الفريق قبل ساعات من المباراة، حقق بداية مثالية في مسيرته مع الهلال، حيث اعتمد على مزيج من اللاعبين المخضرمين والشباب. يعتبر الهلال المرشح الأبرز لتصدر مجموعته والتأهل إلى المرحلة النهائية من الدوري، حيث سيواجه هلال كريمة في الجولة الثانية مطلع ديسمبر. هذا الفوز يعزز آمال جماهير الهلال في الاحتفاظ باللقب، ويعكس قوة الفريق في بداية الموسم.
